title: Method Shorthand Syntax Considered Harmful: why to avoid bivariant method signatures in TypeScript
summary: Matt Pocock explains that TypeScript's method shorthand syntax is bivariant, letting a narrower parameter type slip through and cause runtime errors the compiler never flags. Declaring members as function properties makes the check strict, and the typescript-eslint method-signature-style rule enforces it.

principles.text: Avoid method shorthand syntax in interfaces and types in almost all cases; it can cause runtime errors TypeScript won't catch.
principles.quote: method shorthand syntax should be avoided in almost all cases.

principles.text: Method shorthand is bivariant, so it accepts parameter types narrower or wider than declared, which is the source of the unsound runtime errors.
principles.quote: This happens because the method shorthand syntax is _bivariant_. This means that the method can accept a type that is both narrower and wider than the original type.

principles.text: Declare function members with object property syntax so TypeScript rejects narrower parameter types that would break at runtime.
principles.quote: If we use object property syntax to define the method, TypeScript will throw an error if we try to assign a narrower type to the method

principles.text: The shorthand-vs-property difference has nothing to do with arrow functions versus function declarations; both work with either syntax.
principles.quote: A common misconception is that the syntax above refers to arrow functions vs function declarations. This is not the case.

principles.text: The problem occurs with both interface and type aliases, so switching between them doesn't avoid it.
principles.quote: I've used `interface` in the example above, but the same problem occurs with `type`

principles.text: Enforce the property style with the @typescript-eslint/method-signature-style rule set to "property".
principles.quote: This rule will enforce the use of the object property syntax for method signatures.
